title: Owensboro / Yellow Banks
summary: Owensboro grew from Yellow Banks, an Ohio River landing where Bill Smothers built a cabin about 1797, and was incorporated as Owensborough in 1817.
bodyMarkdown:
Long before it had a town name, a stretch of high clay bluff on the south bank of the [Ohio River](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ohio_River) gave river travelers a landmark. Flatboat crews called the landing Yellow Banks for the color of the clay. The site offered a stopping point on one of the busiest water roads into the West.

About 1797, frontiersman [William Smeathers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Smeathers), better known as Bill Smothers, built a cabin there and became the first settler of what is now [Owensboro](https://grokipedia.com/page/Owensboro,_Kentucky). Smothers already knew the Green River country. He had been an early settler at Fort Hartford on the Rough River, [a story told here](/stories/hartford-fort-hartford-on-the-rough-river/), and helped build a fort at Vienna, later Calhoun, in the early 1780s.

Other families followed, and by around 1800 a small farming and trading community had gathered at the landing. The settlers chose the bluff for its access to river trade, even though the steep banks made landing goods difficult.

Government caught up in stages. The [Kentucky General Assembly](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kentucky_General_Assembly) created [Daviess County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Daviess_County,_Kentucky) in 1815, and the town was laid out in streets and lots in 1816. In 1817 it was incorporated as Owensborough. The name honored Col. Abraham Owen, a Kentucky legislator and militia officer killed at the [Battle of Tippecanoe](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Tippecanoe) in 1811. The spelling was shortened to Owensboro in 1893.

Smothers did not stay. He later moved to Texas, and in 1821 he helped [Stephen F. Austin](https://grokipedia.com/page/Stephen_F._Austin) explore the Texas coast to choose a site for his first colony. In 1822 he was one of five men who built a fort at a bend of the Brazos River, the post that gave Fort Bend County its name.

The story of Owensboro's start is a common one along the Ohio. A landing known to boatmen became a cabin, then a cluster of farms, then a county seat with a planned grid. Each step tied the river bank more closely to the new state's courts and markets.

## Kentucky today

Owensboro is the seat of Daviess County and one of Kentucky's largest cities. Smothers Park on the downtown riverfront is named for the first settler and sits near the old Yellow Banks landing. Visitors can walk the riverfront and look across the same stretch of the Ohio that drew flatboats more than two centuries ago.
